title: Implement the quick sort algorithm, explain the partition step and pivot choice, and analyse its time complexity.

s1_definition.profdef: Quick sort is a divide-and-conquer, comparison-based sorting algorithm. It picks a pivot element, partitions the array so that everything smaller than the pivot sits to its left and everything larger to its right, then recursively sorts the two partitions. It sorts in place with logarithmic extra space for the recursion, runs in n log n time on average, but degrades to quadratic time if pivots are consistently poor.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India must sort a pile of transactions by amount. A clerk grabs one transaction as a reference, the pivot, and splits the pile into "smaller than the pivot" on the left and "larger than the pivot" on the right, placing the pivot exactly between them where it now belongs forever. She then repeats the same splitting independently on the left pile and the right pile, and keeps going until every small pile has one item. Because each item lands in its correct zone early, the whole pile ends up sorted without ever needing a separate second pile to copy into.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pick a pivot, partition smaller-left and larger-right, then recursively sort each side in place.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Quick sort is a divide-and-conquer, comparison-based sorting algorithm. It picks a pivot element, partitions the array so that everything smaller than the pivot sits to its left and everything larger to its right, then recursively sorts the two partitions. It sorts in place with logarithmic extra space for the recursion, runs in n log n time on average, but degrades to quadratic time if pivots are consistently poor.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India must sort a pile of transactions by amount. A clerk grabs one transaction as a reference, the pivot, and splits the pile into "smaller than the pivot" on the left and "larger than the pivot" on the right, placing the pivot exactly between them where it now belongs forever. She then repeats the same splitting independently on the left pile and the right pile, and keeps going until every small pile has one item. Because each item lands in its correct zone early, the whole pile ends up sorted without ever needing a separate second pile to copy into.

**One line to remember:** Pick a pivot, partition smaller-left and larger-right, then recursively sort each side in place.

sections.s2_technical:
The heart of quick sort is the partition step, which does the real work; the recursion just applies it to shrinking ranges. Partition chooses a pivot and rearranges the current sub-array so the pivot ends in its final sorted position, with all smaller elements before it and all larger after it. A common scheme, the Lomuto partition, uses the last element as pivot and a boundary index that marks the end of the "smaller" region: you scan the range, and whenever an element is less than the pivot you swap it into the boundary and advance the boundary, then finally swap the pivot into the boundary slot.

Once partition returns the pivot's final index, you recurse on the left part, from the start up to just before the pivot, and the right part, from just after the pivot to the end. The pivot itself is never touched again because it is already correctly placed. The recursion ends when a range has zero or one element, which is trivially sorted. Crucially there is no merge step, unlike merge sort, because the partitioning already arranges elements relative to each other, which is why quick sort sorts in place.

The complexity hinges entirely on pivot quality. With balanced partitions, each level processes n elements and there are about log n levels, giving n log n. But if the pivot is always the smallest or largest, for example choosing the last element on already-sorted input, partitions are maximally unbalanced, producing n levels and quadratic time. The classic defences are to choose the pivot well: median-of-three sampling, or a randomised pivot that makes the bad case astronomically unlikely regardless of input order. Randomisation is the standard production safeguard.

A senior-level nuance is that quick sort is not stable, meaning equal elements can be reordered, and it is cache-friendly with small constant factors, which is why it is often the fastest in practice and underlies primitive-array sorting via a dual-pivot variant in Java's Arrays.sort. For objects Java uses a stable merge-based TimSort instead, precisely because quick sort is unstable. I use median-of-three or randomisation whenever input order is adversarial or unknown.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must sort a large in-memory array of transaction amounts quickly and without allocating a second large array, because memory is tight on the processing node. Quick sort's in-place partitioning fits this exactly.

Problem 2 — Transaction feeds can arrive nearly sorted, which is the worst case for a naive last-element pivot, so we must guard against quadratic blow-up. Choosing the pivot by median-of-three keeps partitions balanced even on sorted-ish input.

In our mini-project we build an `AmountSorter` that sorts an integer array of amounts in place using quick sort with a median-of-three pivot. The demo sorts an unsorted array and logs the result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the amounts fifty thousand, one thousand two hundred, ninety eight thousand, three hundred, seven thousand five hundred, twenty five thousand, four hundred.

Step 1: Call quick sort on the whole range. Partition picks a pivot by median-of-three of the first, middle, and last elements, parks it at the end, and scans.

Step 2: During the scan, every element smaller than the pivot is swapped into the growing "smaller" region at the front, and the boundary advances. Larger elements are left in place to the right.

Step 3: After the scan, the pivot is swapped into the boundary slot, which is its final sorted position. All smaller amounts now sit to its left and all larger to its right.

Step 4: Quick sort recurses on the left sub-array of smaller amounts. The same partition logic settles another pivot into place and splits that part further.

Step 5: Quick sort recurses on the right sub-array of larger amounts, settling pivots there too. The recursion keeps halving the ranges until each has one element, which needs no work.

Step 6: Because every pivot was placed in its final position and the two sides were sorted independently in place, the full array is now sorted ascending, three hundred, four hundred, one thousand two hundred, seven thousand five hundred, twenty five thousand, fifty thousand, ninety eight thousand, with no second array allocated.

```
[2026-10-26 23:40:01] INFO    Sorted amounts: [300, 400, 1200, 7500, 25000, 50000, 98000]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Quick sort is a divide-and-conquer, comparison-based sort. It picks a pivot, partitions the array so everything smaller than the pivot is to its left and everything larger is to its right, which places the pivot in its final sorted position, and then recursively sorts the two partitions. It sorts in place using only logarithmic extra space for the recursion stack, and it does not need a merge step because the partitioning already arranges elements relative to each other.

The heart of the algorithm is the partition step; the recursion just applies it to shrinking ranges. In the Lomuto scheme I keep a boundary that marks the end of the smaller region, scan the range, and whenever I see an element less than the pivot I swap it into the boundary and advance the boundary, then finally swap the pivot into the boundary slot. Partition returns the pivot's final index, and I recurse on the elements before it and the elements after it. The recursion bottoms out when a range has zero or one element.

The complexity depends entirely on pivot quality. With balanced partitions it is n log n, but if the pivot is consistently the smallest or largest, which happens with a naive last-element pivot on already-sorted data, the partitions are maximally unbalanced and it degrades to quadratic. In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used quick sort to sort large in-memory arrays of transaction amounts without allocating a second array, and because the feeds often arrive nearly sorted, I chose the pivot by median-of-three to keep the partitions balanced and avoid that worst case; randomising the pivot is the equivalent production safeguard.

The senior-level point I make is that quick sort is not stable, so equal elements can be reordered, which is exactly why Java uses a dual-pivot quick sort for primitive arrays in Arrays.sort but a stable merge-based TimSort for object arrays where preserving order matters. Quick sort wins in practice for primitives because it is in place and cache-friendly with small constant factors, so I reach for it when stability does not matter and memory is tight, while guarding the pivot choice against adversarial input.
